@graph.headline: The 3-Day Rule: A Circuit Breaker for Consecutive Losing Days
@graph.description: Three consecutive red days? Take three market days away from the screens. The complete 3-day rule protocol — trigger, break, and staged return ladder.

mainEntity.name: What is the 3-day rule in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: After three consecutive losing days, take a mandatory three-day break from trading — three market days off, no live positions, review only. It is a pre-committed circuit breaker: you sign the rule while calm so it binds you when you're tilted. Note the investor variant: some investors use "3-day rule" to mean waiting three days before buying a stock that dropped hard — same family (imposed distance), different problem.

mainEntity.name: Should you stop trading after a losing streak?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you're a discretionary trader whose decision quality degrades under emotional load — yes. Three red days is the point where loss-aversion compounding, tilt, and revenge/overtrading loops typically ignite. The break interrupts the emotional feedback loop and protects the account from tilt-driven damage. Systematic traders with valid stop-outs are the honest exception — for them, skipping trades is the deviation.

mainEntity.name: How many consecutive losses before you stop trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three tiers: intraday, most experienced traders end the session after 2–4 consecutive full-stop losses (three is the common landing point); at the day level, three consecutive red days triggers the 3-day rule — three market days off. The daily-loss-limit tier (dollar-based, intraday) and the 3-day rule (day-count based, multi-day) stack: the loss limit ends the session, the 3-day rule ends the stretch.

mainEntity.name: How long should a trading break be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minimum 24 hours after three consecutive losses; the 3-day rule takes three full market days (review-only). A full reset needs distance, not a nap — one weekend rarely discharges three red days of emotional charge. Market days are trading days: NSE holidays don't count as break days.

mainEntity.name: What should you do during a trading break?

acceptedAnswer.text: Day 1: complete distance — no charts, no scanning, no paper trading. Day 2: structured review — log all three days' trades and answer three questions (did I follow my rules? were the setups valid? bad process or bad luck?), separating poor executions from valid statistical stop-outs. Day 3: check whether the market regime changed, then run 2–3 calm demo trades to verify clean execution.

mainEntity.name: How do you know when to return to trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the staged return ladder: review-only → demo-verified (2–3 clean paper trades) → half size live (0.2–0.5% risk for a few sessions) → full size only when execution is clean across sessions. One green day doesn't end probation; one red day at half size restarts it. Full size is earned back with evidence, not hope.

mainEntity.name: Why can't I stop trading after losing?

acceptedAnswer.text: The state-machine problem: the calm version of you writes the plan, and a different, emotionally flooded version executes it under pressure. That future self won't be persuaded in the moment — which is why the rule must be pre-committed, written down physically, witnessed by someone, and ideally made structural (a calendar block, the app deleted for three days). You don't negotiate with the tilted self; you bind them in advance.

mainEntity.name: Does the 3-day rule apply to systematic or algo traders?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — and that's stated honestly. A backtested system with positive expectancy doesn't care about streaks; if all three red days were clean, rule-following executions, skipping the next trades is itself the deviation. The rule protects discretionary decision quality. It cannot improve a process with no discretion in it.

mainEntity.name: Is a 3-day break different from a daily loss limit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The daily loss limit is dollar-based and intraday — it protects the *day*. The 3-day rule is day-count based and multi-day — it protects the *week and the month*. They stack: the loss limit ends the session, the 3-day rule ends the stretch.
